title: Storage and Distributed Systems
description: Persistence, consistency, fault tolerance, and distributed-system trade-offs.

questions.prompt: In ACID transactions, what does durability promise?
options: Committed changes survive failures according to the system’s guarantees
Every query returns in constant time
questions.explanation: Durability means committed effects persist across specified failures, often using logs or replicated storage.

questions.prompt: What does transaction atomicity mean?
options: A transaction’s operations all take effect or none do
Every read returns the newest global value
questions.explanation: Atomicity prevents partial transaction effects from being exposed as committed state.

questions.prompt: Serializable isolation aims for results equivalent to some serial transaction order.
questions.explanation: A serializable execution preserves the effect of running transactions one at a time in some order.

questions.prompt: Why use a write-ahead log?
options: Record changes before applying them so recovery can restore consistency
questions.explanation: The log provides a recovery record that can be replayed or used to undo incomplete updates.

questions.prompt: What is data replication?
options: Maintaining copies of data on multiple nodes
Splitting one file into source-code functions
questions.explanation: Replicas can improve availability or read performance, while introducing coordination and consistency concerns.

questions.prompt: Replicated copies are always immediately identical after every write.
questions.explanation: Replication may be asynchronous, so replicas can temporarily lag or diverge during failures.

questions.prompt: In a replicated system, what does a quorum generally mean?
options: A required number of nodes must participate in an operation
Every node must always be online
The database stores only one copy
questions.explanation: Quorum rules require enough replicas for reads or writes to meet a chosen consistency and availability design.

questions.prompt: What does eventual consistency promise, assuming updates stop and communication recovers?
options: Replicas will converge to a consistent value eventually
Every read immediately returns the latest write
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence but expects replicas to converge when updates cease and messages are delivered.

questions.prompt: Which are common failure modes in distributed systems?
options: A global clock with perfect synchronization
questions.explanation: Partitions, node failures, and duplicate delivery are common; perfect global clocks are not a safe assumption.

questions.prompt: What property makes a retry safe for an operation?
options: Repeating it has the same effect as performing it once
questions.explanation: Idempotent operations can be retried without duplicating their intended effect.

questions.prompt: Why is “exactly once” processing difficult in distributed systems?
options: Failures can leave uncertainty about whether an operation already took effect
Messages are always delivered in order
questions.explanation: A sender may not know whether a timed-out request committed; deduplication and idempotent design help manage this uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which techniques can improve fault tolerance?
questions.explanation: Replication and error detection address some failures; retries should be bounded and designed to avoid overload.

questions.prompt: Why use exponential backoff with jitter for retries?
options: Reduce synchronized retry spikes and spread load
questions.explanation: Backoff slows repeated attempts, while jitter avoids many clients retrying in lockstep.

questions.prompt: Why is cache invalidation challenging?
options: Keeping cached data consistent with changing source data is difficult
questions.explanation: Stale entries are hard to manage because updates and cached copies can race across components.

questions.prompt: A cache is generally a substitute for durable primary storage.
questions.explanation: Caches optimize access and may be evicted; durable storage is responsible for preserving authoritative data.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a natural fit for object storage?
options: Large unstructured objects addressed by keys
questions.explanation: Object stores handle durable blobs such as media and backups, typically via object identifiers and metadata.

questions.prompt: What does block storage expose to a host?
options: A volume of fixed-size addressable blocks
questions.explanation: Block storage presents raw blocks that a host can format with a filesystem or use directly.

questions.prompt: Which are sound backup practices?
options: Keep backups isolated from routine credentials
Retain versions according to recovery needs
Assume successful backup logs prove restore works
questions.explanation: Isolation, retention, and restore tests improve recovery; a backup is useful only if it can be restored.

questions.prompt: What does recovery point objective (RPO) describe?
options: The maximum acceptable data loss measured in time
The maximum time to restore service
questions.explanation: RPO defines how far back recovery may need to go, expressing tolerance for lost recent data.

questions.prompt: What does recovery time objective (RTO) describe?
options: The target time to restore a service after disruption
questions.explanation: RTO specifies the target duration for restoring service after an outage.
